clue.text: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter

definitions.text: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter

parts.words: Such a clue's ideal for a letter-sorter
parts.note: a solver who likes rearranging letters is best served by a clue whose wordplay asks for exactly that shuffling

explanation.surface: A remark about which kind of crossword clue suits someone who sorts letters, perhaps at a post office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter-sorter' suggests a postal worker sorting mail, but the letters here are the alphabet's, and the clue type that sorts them is the one named.
explanation.definitionFit: A clue built from rearranged letters is described by this adjective, the kind of clue a letter-juggler enjoys.

clue.text: Play part, over a long time, of one hounded to death

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, on top of, the second

parts.note: an act is a part of a play
an aeon is an immensely long time

explanation.surface: An actor who plays a role for ages, in a story about someone hunted down.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Actaeon saw Artemis bathing; she turned him into a stag and his own hounds tore him apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hunter was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own dogs, so he was literally hounded to death.

clue.text: Concede it has a little mark on it

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set on another comes above it

parts.note: DM is the short form of the Deutschmark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: Someone admitting a small blemish on an object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' is the German currency, and 'little' shortens it to its abbreviation DM; A and DM sit 'on' IT in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit a point is to concede or acknowledge it as true.

clue.text: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies

definitions.text: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies

parts.words: More heavenly joy from this baddie than from 99 goodies
parts.note: the Gospel says heaven rejoices more over one sinner who turns away from sin than over ninety-nine righteous people

explanation.surface: A comic reckoning of heaven's preference for a reformed villain over a crowd of good people.
explanation.walkthrough: Luke 15:7: 'joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sinner who is sorry and turns from wrongdoing is the one the parable says brings heaven more joy.

clue.text: Average-sounding air

indicators.note: the word for average is only heard, giving a word spoken the same way

parts.note: the mean is an average

explanation.surface: A tune or atmosphere that comes across as merely ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' is not a tune here but a person's manner or bearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's air is their bearing or manner, the look they present.

clue.text: Statesman

parts.note: read as States man, a man from the United States

explanation.definitionFit: Split into two words, the clue gives a man of the States, a US citizen.

clue.text: The-fashionable crowd does not take up the whole page

definitions.meaning: the fashionable people, those who are 'in'

definitions.text: does not take up the whole page
definitions.meaning: a small picture or map set within a larger page

explanation.walkthrough: Split, the answer is IN SET, the trendy crowd; whole, it is a small panel set into a page.
explanation.definitionFit: The trendy social group is the in-set, and a small panel within a larger printed page or map is likewise an inset.

clue.text: Bellman hunted with him

parts.note: in the Cumbrian hunting song 'D'ye ken ...', Bellman is one of the hounds who ran with the huntsman

explanation.surface: A town crier who went hunting with some companion.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'D'ye ken John Peel' names the hounds 'Ranter and Ringwood, Bellman and True'. A bellman is usually a town crier, the false lead.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Cumberland huntsman of the folk song hunted with a hound named Bellman.

clue.text: Superior quarter-on which we may find beggars

definitions.meaning: the upper part of a shoe, including the quarter at its back, sits above the sole

definitions.text: on which we may find beggars
definitions.meaning: to be 'on one's ...' is to be penniless, worn down to the shoe tops

explanation.walkthrough: A shoe's 'quarter' is the part of its upper round the heel; 'on one's uppers' means destitute, the soles worn through.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe tops are the higher parts above the sole, and being on them is the idiom for poverty.

clue.text: Quarter of an 'hour for instance by this

definitions.text: Quarter of an 'hour for instance by this

parts.words: Quarter of an 'hour for instance by this
parts.note: a quarter of an hour is a piece of time, and a clock is the thing you tell such a quarter by

explanation.surface: Someone checking that fifteen minutes have passed by glancing at something.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as TIME PIECE: a quarter of an hour is literally a piece of time, and a clock is also what you read the quarter by.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock or watch is a device for keeping time, and its name splits into a phrase meaning a portion of time.

clue.text: In the Cheshire Cheese perhaps, it's exclusive in Fleet Street

definitions.meaning: a Cheshire cheese is served with a ladle-like tool for digging out portions; Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is also a famous Fleet Street pub
Fleet Street, the old home of London's newspapers, calls a story one paper has alone by this name

explanation.walkthrough: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is a pub on Fleet Street, London's former newspaper district, so the whole clue reads as journalists' gossip in their local.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheese is dug out with a small shovel-like tool, and a newspaper's exclusive story is the journalist's word for a story nobody else has.

clue.text: The Mouse-trap's story "——, and writ in very choice Italian"

parts.words: and writ in very choice Italian
parts.note: this completes Hamlet's line about the play he calls The Mousetrap, which says its story still survives in fine Italian writing

explanation.surface: A line about a play's source, quoted from a famous tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet (Act III scene ii) Hamlet says of The Murder of Gonzago, which he renames The Mousetrap: 'The story is extant, and writ in very choice Italian'. The missing word fills the blank.
explanation.definitionFit: A story that still survives in existence is one that has not been lost, which is what Hamlet claims for the play's source.

clue.text: Length of a ball, including its break

indicators.note: the dance word takes the scrambled letters inside it

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: to break the word its is to scatter its three letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A cricket or tennis ball's flight measured, spin and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like the spin on a cricket ball, but it is the anagram signal on 'its', and 'including' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A distance is a length between two points.

clue.text: 36.9 .degrees centigrade is not unusual

definitions.meaning: roughly the healthy human body temperature, the reading a doctor calls standard

explanation.walkthrough: 36.9 degrees Celsius is about the temperature of a healthy body, so a thermometer showing it is said to read the standard value.
explanation.definitionFit: Healthy body temperature is called standard, and anything ordinary or usual is described the same way.

clue.text: Fashion houses make no bones about' the Steptoe business

definitions.text: Fashion houses make no bones about' the Steptoe business

parts.words: Fashion houses make no bones about' the Steptoe business
parts.note: Steptoe and Son were TV rag-and-bone men; the fashion industry deals in clothes but leaves out the bones

explanation.surface: Fashion houses being frank about a TV junk dealer's firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Steptoe and Son was a British sitcom about rag-and-bone men, who collected old clothes and scrap; drop the bones and the trade is in rags only.
explanation.definitionFit: The clothing and fashion industry is colloquially called the rag trade.

clue.text: Saint consumes a quarter of bread that's sweet?

indicators.note: the saint's name swallows the compass letter, so it sits inside

parts.note: St Pancras is a saint, known to Londoners from the railway station named after him
east is one of the four quarters of the compass, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: A holy man eating a slice of a loaf that tastes sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A quarter of bread' looks like a portion of a loaf; 'a quarter' is the compass point E, and 'bread that's sweet' is sweetbread, the culinary name for this gland.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetbread is the cooks' name for an animal's pancreas or thymus served as food, so the gland is a sweet bread.

clue.text: Far from dim over the bar

definitions.text: Far from dim over the bar

parts.words: Far from dim over the bar
parts.note: 'dim' is the musical abbreviation for getting softer, and the opposite marking written above the bars of music means getting louder

explanation.surface: A pub that is brightly lit above its counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like a lighting level and 'bar' like a pub; in music dim. marks diminuendo, and its opposite is written over the bars of a score.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical direction for a gradual increase in loudness is the opposite of diminuendo, and is marked over the music.

clue.text: Cock Robin death report 'such pathos!

parts.note: in the nursery rhyme all the birds fell a-sighing and a-sobbing at the death of Cock Robin, a report full of tearful sentiment

explanation.surface: Someone moved by the nursery rhyme account of a bird's killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who Killed Cock Robin?' ends with all the birds 'a-sighing and a-sobbing' when they hear the bell toll.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing designed to make readers weep is dismissed as mawkish, tear-jerking material.

clue.text: Devils, self-styled, round at diplomat's house

indicators.note: the devils' name goes round the little word, holding it inside

parts.note: in the Gospels the demons possessing a man call themselves Legion, 'for we are many'

explanation.surface: Self-proclaimed demons gathering around an embassy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Mark 5:9 the unclean spirits answer 'My name is Legion: for we are many', which is how the devils styled themselves; 'round' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A legation is a diplomatic mission and the building that houses the minister and staff.

clue.text: Chairman's pet

parts.note: read as chair-man, a person sitting in a chair, whose pet curls up on their knees

explanation.surface: The favourite of a company boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chairman's pet' suggests a boardroom favourite; it is the small dog that sits on the seated person's knees.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pet dog kept to sit on its owner's knees as they sit is also a word for a fawning favourite.

clue.text: Tom was crazy to go there

definitions.text: Tom was crazy to go there

parts.words: Tom was crazy to go there
parts.note: Tom o' ... was the stock name for a madman released from London's old asylum, so a crazy Tom was sent there

explanation.surface: Someone remarking that a friend called Tom was foolish to visit some place.
explanation.walkthrough: Bethlem Royal Hospital in London was the old madhouse; its former inmates who begged on the roads were called 'Tom o' Bedlam'.
explanation.definitionFit: The London lunatic asylum gave its nickname to any scene of uproar and madness, the place where mad people were sent.

clue.text: One in charge is perhaps a German

indicators.note: perhaps tells us the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Speculation that a boss may be German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals rearranging A GERMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a business or team is its boss.

clue.text: He takes off from Port Said, sort of

indicators.note: the letters of the port's name are given a sort, rearranged into another order

explanation.surface: A traveller departing from the Egyptian port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes off' looks like a plane leaving Port Said, but it means mimics; 'sort of' asks for the letters of PORT SAID to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who mimics or imitates for comic effect writes or performs a mocking imitation, a parody.

clue.text: His artful signature suggesting anno domini

definitions.text: His artful signature suggesting anno domini

parts.words: His artful signature suggesting anno domini
parts.note: the German Renaissance artist signed with a monogram of his initials, A over D, which also stand for anno domini

explanation.surface: A signature that seems to give a date in the Christian era.
explanation.walkthrough: Albrecht Dürer signed his prints with a monogram of a large A over a small D, the same letters as AD for anno domini.
explanation.definitionFit: Albrecht the German engraver used the initials AD as his signature, the same as the abbreviation for the year of our Lord.

clue.text: Riddle for star-gazers

definitions.meaning: a riddle is a coarse sieve, as for sifting soil or gravel
film fans gazing at movie stars watch them on the cinema's big white surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' means a coarse sieve, not a puzzle; 'star-gazers' are film fans, not astronomers.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen is a mesh for sifting, like a riddle, and the surface where films and their stars are shown.

clue.text: Supplementing a note with a sovereign?

parts.note: E is a musical note
a king is a sovereign ruler

explanation.surface: Paying with a gold coin to top up a banknote.
explanation.walkthrough: A note and a sovereign look like money (a sovereign is a gold coin), but they are the musical note E and a king.
explanation.definitionFit: Eking out means supplementing a meagre supply to make it last.

clue.text: Victim of the firstborn

parts.note: in Genesis, Adam and Eve's eldest son Cain murdered his younger brother

explanation.surface: Someone harmed by the eldest child of a family.
explanation.walkthrough: Cain was the first son born to Adam and Eve, and he killed his brother.
explanation.definitionFit: The second son of Adam and Eve was killed by Cain, the first child born, in Genesis.

clue.text: We get this day by day

definitions.text: We get this day by day

parts.words: We get this day by day
parts.note: each passing day adds to everyone's age, so we all grow more aged daily

explanation.surface: A comment about something received every day, like a daily newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Each passing day makes a person more advanced in years than before.

clue.text: Bun cooked to a finish but so stiff!

indicators.note: the bun is cooked, so its letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: an ending is a finish

explanation.surface: A bun baked right through until it has gone hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like baking but is the anagram signal on 'Bun'; 'to' and 'but so' are only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unbending is rigid and will not flex, which is to say stiff.

clue.text: Dawkins .J would make a crafty fly-half

definitions.meaning: Jack Dawkins is the pickpocket in Dickens's Oliver Twist, known by his nickname
a cunning rugby fly-half who sidesteps tacklers would be an ...

explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dawkins is the Artful Dodger of Oliver Twist; a fly-half is the rugby player who directs attacks, and a crafty one dodges tackles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dickens pickpocket's nickname means a crafty evader, which also suits a slippery rugby fly-half.
